title: Dogen's Japan Journals, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Master Dogen shared teachings from his Chinese teacher Rujing on practical aspects of zazen practice, emphasizing the importance of maintaining awareness without attachment while letting go of all ideas of who we are. This "dropping off body and mind" concept allows for a more authentic and compassionate practice, where one can cultivate flexibility of mind and heart. By releasing attachments to our conceptual selves, we can tap into a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world, recognizing impermanence as a fundamental aspect of reality that leads to compassion and interconnectedness.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Thanks for being here.
We seem to keep showing up.
I'm just going to assume there's a good reason.
Keep coming.
Well, for a third time, and I think the last time, we'll explore a little bit more from Master Dogen's journal about his time in China with his Chinese teacher Rujing in his mid-20s.
Just briefly to recall, this was an undated text found after his death by his attendant, by his jisha, Ejo.
And I'll read you the [unclear: "call of fun"] at the end.
It's very sweet.
He was quite moved to find this.
And you would be, wouldn't you?
This teacher you'd studied and lived with for decades, really intimate and close with them, but with a certain degree of formality, I'm sure.
But then tidying up their room to find a beautiful journal.
That's been quite a moment.
If it was a journal, that we're not really sure.
It's possible Dogen wrote it as a kind of retrospective imagining of his time in China, to explain a little more his understanding.
We don't know.
Who knows?
His conversations included plenty of subtle philosophical discussion, which I tried to touch on a little bit, and some really practical stuff, too.
So I thought let's do a few practical ones.
*Rujing instructed me, when you do zazen, place your tongue on the roof of your mouth.
Allow it to press behind the front teeth.
If after 40 or 50 years of zazen practice, you are accustomed to sitting without drooping and becoming drowsy, then it will be all right to close your eyes.*
That was great.
For those not so accustomed to zazen, less than 40 or 50 years, we should sit with the eyes open.
*You sit long and are tired.
It's all right to shift the position of your legs.
This has been directly transmitted by the Buddha for 50 generations.*
So that's why we don't close our eyes for quite a while.
*Rujing said, during zazen, do not lean against the wall, the screen, or the back of the chair.
If you do, it will cause you to become ill.
You should sit with straight back, following the guidelines for zazen, never violating them.*
I thought that was interesting, to hear that they did sit in chairs.
So there's instruction there for sitting zazen in a chair: sit upright in the chair.

And I always feel like I should modify or say something about the perfect descriptions of posture in these traditional texts, because it would be pretty easy for us to stress ourselves out trying to, you know, like this.
I've tried it.
You probably have too.
It doesn't work out very well.
But we make some effort to be upright, to be awake.
But please let it be gentle.
The place to fix your posture is not so much on the cushion; it's like at the chiropractor's or the [unclear: "ralthing place"].
But you make an effort to be upright with the body that you ended up with.
Anyway, more from Rujing, more practical stuff.
*If you get up from zazen to do walking meditation, do not walk in a circle, but go in a straight line.
If after 20 or 30 steps you want to turn around, always turn to the right and always begin your steps with the right foot, then the left foot.*
There's just endless refinement here, isn't there?
Which foot did you begin with tonight?
You don't know?
Oh.
You're just assuming you did it wrong, basically.
Another time, Rujing was also talking about kinhin.
*When you get up from zazen to walk, you should practice the method of slow walking meditation.
Do not go more than half a step with each breath.*
So this is an old tradition we're trying to live into here, going so slow.
Another time, Rujing said about zazen:
*In zazen, it is possible to develop samadhi by placing the mind in various locations.
However, I would say during zazen, you should set your mind on the palm of your left hand, which is the one on top.
This is the way correctly transmitted by Buddha ancestors.*
So in the mudra.
Actually, Sojun Mel Weitsman used to recommend this.
I remember him saying this: put your mind in your hands, put your mind in your mudra and really pay attention to your mudra.
Possibly Suzuki Roshi said that to him.
There are also some interesting suggestions, not just about the practical technique of all this, but also about the spirit and the feeling of the practice.
Sometimes a little poetical or a little indirect, but this one, I think, is very direct.
*Rujing said, the world honored one, this is the Buddha, said that hearing and thinking about the way is like being outside the gate.
But zazen is like coming home and sitting calmly inside.
Therefore the merit of doing zazen even for one moment is immeasurable.
I have been practicing the way for over 30 years without ever turning back.
And although I am 65 years old, I am more determined than ever.
You should practice with this intensity as if you had received the prediction of enlightenment from the golden mouth of Buddha himself.*
And that's a feature in many of the Mahayana Sutras.

One of the things that happens in the career, the many-lifetime career of a bodhisattva who is heading towards Buddhahood, is that when you get pretty close, you somehow run into a Buddha and the Buddha predicts that you will be a Buddha someday.
So that's a thing that happens.
So imagine that that had happened and sit with that.
He says intensity, at least it's translated as intensity.
And of course, we can change it a little bit: devotion, ease, love, joy, with some energy.
With our hands, I just put my hands upside down, our minds in our palms and Buddha's golden mouth whispering in our ears.
Beautiful, huh?
Another one about the spirit of this.
And here he's going to do a little comparing with other styles of Buddhism.
*The zazen of arhats and pratyekabuddhas is free from attachment, but it lacks all-embracing compassion.
This is very different from the zazen of Buddha ancestors, where all-embracing compassion and the vow to awaken all sentient beings is the highest priority.*
So arhats and Prachekha Buddhas represent early Buddhism, where the ideal is a little more just chilling out in a very deep, profound way: stillness and peace.
So they're free from attachment.
That's great.
But the compassion isn't there in this way of looking at it.
He goes on:
*People outside the way in India, so non-Buddhists, also practice zazen, but this zazen still has the three problems of attachments, wrong views and pride.
So it is utterly different from the zazen of Buddha ancestors.
Shravakas also practice zazen.
It's another style of practice, but their compassion is limited.
They do not penetrate the reality of all with wisdom.
Instead, they improve themselves and thus remove themselves from the creative seed of the Buddhas.
So their zazen too is utterly different from that of Buddha ancestors.*
That's pretty interesting, huh?
So if you're getting into self-improvement, you've created some separation from all this.
You've removed yourself from the creative seed of the Buddhas.
I don't know in which sense they meant seed there.
He goes on:
*The very essence of Buddha ancestors' zazen is the vow to accumulate Buddha qualities from the moment of arousing the aspiration for enlightenment into the endless future.
Buddha ancestors never forget or abandon sentient beings.
They have compassion for all creatures, even insects, and make a constant effort to save them all.
And they turn over whatever merit is produced from their practice to sentient beings.
Because of this vow, Buddha ancestors always practice zazen in the desire realm.*
So in this mixed-up place is where we practice, in our everyday world, which has great opportunities for influencing cause and effect.
*Buddha ancestors practice this way life after life, world after world, and attain great flexibility of mind and heart.*
So that was all Rujing speaking.
Then Dogen says:
*I bowed and said, how do we attain this flexibility of mind and heart?
Rujing said, to actualize Buddha ancestors' dropping off body and mind is the essence of this flexibility.
That's why dropping off body and mind is called the mind seal of Buddha ancestors.
I bow deeply.*
Thank you.
So this is a little bit of a confusing phrase.
It's a favorite of Dogen's, which obviously he got in China from Rujing.

Some kind of deep release, letting go of our idea, all ideas of who we are, letting go of the separation between self and other, because you're letting go of the idea there is such a thing as self and other: dropping away body and mind.
It means awakening.
So that's a little more complicated, but about the spirit of this, that it's about compassion and letting go.
And then one more in this theme.
Rujing really encouraged young Dogen to really feel the presence of the ancestors.
That's a really tangible thing, not just an idea.
He said:
*The ruins of the place where the Tathagata got up from zazen and did walking meditation still exist in the [unclear: "Udanya"] kingdom in India.
Also layman Vimalakirti's house still exists today.
And the foundation stones of [unclear: "Jeddah"] Grove monastery have not been buried.
And when people go to examine these sacred places, the results of their measures really differ.
Some measure long, some measure short.
Some find the stones close together, others find them farther apart.
And their findings correspond.
And this is the vitality of the Buddha ancestors.*
Those are scenes from famous Buddhist stories.
So these places still exist, but there's something dynamic about them, something still changing, something in motion, humming with Dharma.
And so we see it in different ways.
And then he says to Dogen:
*You should know that the bowl and robe as well as the fist and nostrils of the ancestors, which have been transmitted to us in China, cannot be definitively measured.*
It's measureless.
*I stood up and bowed my head to the floor, shedding tears of joy.*
They're strange, but beautiful, aren't they?
And the last thing I want to highlight is a very sweet discussion of a poem that Rujing wrote and which Dogen loved.
And he wrote about it later in his writings.
The poem is called Windbell.
And a windbell is this little bell that hangs in all the eaves of the buildings.
Somebody here has a picture of it in their Zoom screen.
Joan, maybe, yeah.
So next time you're on Zoom, tell Joan to turn off her camera and you can see a windbell.
We saw them all over in Japan, if you look for them.
They're everywhere.
And they only ring if it's pretty windy.
They had some respect for their sanity, because there's a lot of them on the roof.
So here's the poem by Rujing.
*The real body is a mouth hanging in emptiness, whether the wind blows from the east, west, south or north, it joins the whole universe in chiming out prajna.
Ta-ting, ta-ting, ta-ting.*
It's a pretty literal translation.
Here's a little more poetic one by somebody else.
*Whole body like a mouth hanging in space, not asking if the wind is east, west, south or north.
For all others equally, it shatters wisdom.
Chin-ten-tong, in chin-ten-tong.*
It went a little more for the sounds, I guess.
I don't know what the original character is.
You would think somebody wouldn't make up those sounds.
So anyway, that's the poem that Dogen appreciated.
And he asked his teacher about it, this mouth of emptiness, ringing in emptiness.
*I asked my teacher, I heard your voice in the [unclear: "windmill"].
The first line says the entire body is a mouth hanging in emptiness.
And the third line says joining the whole universe and chiming out prajna.
What is this emptiness?
Is it just a lack of form?
People who doubt the way do say this, and nowadays even students of the way do not understand Buddha Dharma.
They regard the spaciousness of the blue sky as emptiness.
This is regrettable.*
And there's an inside joke there.
The Chinese use the same character for sky as for emptiness.
But you can tell by the context which one it is.
*Rujing said, emptiness is no other than prajna, wisdom.
Wisdom.
Emptiness is wisdom.
It's not the lack of form.
Emptiness is neither having nor not having hindrances.
Therefore, it is not emptiness in the sense of lack.
It is not one-sided reality.
Elders in different places have not clarified even form.
How can they clarify*
*I said, well, your verse on the windmill is supreme.
Even if they had numberless eons, our elders would never be able to compose a verse like this.
Brother monks should venerate it.

Although I have come from a remote land and am not well versed in dharma, I have read collections of Zen masters' teachings, like the transmission of the lamp, the wide lamp, the successive lamp, and the universal lamp,* so, big books, *as well as the recorded sayings of the masters.
And I have not seen anything like your windmill verse.
It is my good fortune to have seen it.
I wet my robe with tears of joy and bow down day and night in appreciation of its straightforwardness and beautiful rhythm.*
And it says, *Ru Jing was about to ride off in a sedan chair.* I guess this whole conversation was like in the parking lot.
*He smiled and said, your words are deep and your spirit is outstanding.
I composed this verse when I was at Qingyang Monastery.
At the time, many people praised it, but none of them spoke as you have done.
I acknowledge you have a sharp dharma eye.
When you compose a verse, you should do it in the same manner.*
I love the end of that.
It's wonderfully supportive of the student, isn't it?
So, yeah, thanks.
You have a good eye for poems, and I'm looking forward to hearing yours.
Would you read that?
Yeah.
The translation or the statement?
I'll read the whole thing.
We have time.
Okay, so, the literal translation of the poem.
*The real body is a mouth hanging in emptiness.
When the wind blows from the east, west, south or north, it joins the universe in chiming out prajna, wisdom.*
*Or the whole body like a mouth hanging in space, not asking if the wind is east, west, north or south.
For all others equally, it shatters wisdom.*
So first Dogen asked about the first and third verses: the entire body is a mouth hanging in emptiness, joining the whole universe in chiming out prajna.
He asked like a wonderful beginner question.
This kind of thing makes me wonder if he wrote it later, though.
It's hard to imagine the Dogen we know and love asking something this naive: what is emptiness?
There are fancier ways you could say that.
So it makes me wonder if he was writing it later in life and putting words in his young mouth to make a useful exchange for us to learn from.
I don't know.
But anyway, what is this emptiness?
Is it lack of form?
People say that.
Are they right?
And then Rujing's answer is really a beautiful primer on emptiness, actually.
Emptiness is no other than prajna wisdom.
It's not lack of form.
Emptiness is neither having nor not having hindrances or anything.
Therefore it is not emptiness in the sense of lack.
It is not one-sided reality.
Right?
So if emptiness is beyond conceptual division, you can't say it's not something, right?
So that's already dividing.
You can only say it's kind of not not something.
Elders have not clarified it.
How could we?
Elders have not clarified form.
How could they clarify emptiness?
So it's hard to understand.
And then Dogen praises the verse at great length.
I wonder if the sedan chair carriers, the sedan chair monks, were like, come on, we've got to get going here.
Shut up, Dogen.
*Your verse is supreme.
Even if they had numberless eons, the elders would never compose a verse like this.
Brother monks should venerate it.
Even though I've come from a remote land, I'm not well versed.
I've read the collections and I've never seen anything like your verse.
It's my great fortune to see it.
My robe is wet with tears of joy.
And I bow day and night for this beautiful poem.*
And then Rujing's beautiful reply.
*Your words are deep.
Your spirit is outstanding.
I composed this verse when I was at Jingliang monastery.
And at the time, many people praised it, but none as you have done.
I acknowledge that you have a sharp dharma eye.
And when you compose a verse, you should do it in the same manner.*
It's kind of hard for us, I think, with translated Chinese poetry, because there are very particular styles, and there's probably rhyme and a sort of pattern of the tonality.
You know, they have rising and falling tones.
So it would be beautiful if we had a recording of it being read in Chinese.
And almost always the same number of characters per line.
So it's this block of elegant calligraphy with all these layers of tonality and meaning, and we just have funny old English.
And Dogen did later, in Shobogenzo, especially in this one essay called "Empty Space," about emptiness, quote Ru Jing's poem that he had heard decades before in China.
So here's the colophon.
This is Ejo, his assistant, writing after he's died.
And this was maybe two years after he died.
*On the 10th day, 12th month and 5th year of the Kencho era,* which comes out to 1253, *this was copied in the Abbot's room in the Ehe monastery in Echizen.
The text was found among the late teacher's posthumous documents.
It was in the form of a draft and may not be complete.
I shed many tears and my regret that the work was never completed.*
And so I think what we're supposed to understand from that is that he just copied the whole thing.
There's no photocopier, right?
So that's what you do.
You sit down and copy it, which takes a while, and every stroke, I think, would have a certain meaning.
So I don't have anything too brilliant to say about all this tonight, or themes for discussion, but I'm just curious if you have any thoughts.
Some of you have been to some of these talks, maybe all three of them.
What do you think about hearing all this?
It's interesting, huh?
Getting a sense of Dogen as a person, a young student in China, whether it's a little exaggerated or, you know, retrospectively fabricated.
I don't know if it matters too much.
It gives you that feeling.
Any thoughts?
Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, this poem would be sung.
Yeah.
Oh, that's neat.
Yeah.
So in that last part about the poem.
Oh, yeah, sure.
Sure.
I see, I can find that.
